topics.title_en: Plain / aspirated / tense stops (ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ, ㄷ ㅌ ㄸ, ㅂ ㅍ ㅃ, ㅈ ㅊ ㅉ)
topics.tip_en: Korean has three kinds of stops, not two. Listen for breathiness (ㅋ), tightness (ㄲ), and the plain ㄱ, which is softer, with a lower pitch on the next vowel. Pitch matters as well as breath.
topics.drill_en: Say 가, 카, 까 on your phone recorder; play back and check you hear three clearly different starts, not two.

sources.what_it_says: Yoon & Idemaru (NoWPhon 2016 abstract): contemporary Korean speakers rely heavily on F0 plus VOT for the 3-way stop contrast; L1-Chinese and L1-English learners use F0 as a cue but less robustly than natives, with extensive individual variation.

Han & Kim (2014, Korean Journal of Linguistics): Mandarin-L1 learners over one year picked up VOT control fairly easily but struggled with onset F0; this imbalance affected native listeners' understanding.

Holliday (Korea Univ. record; Language and Speech 2019): naive Japanese listeners heard Korean fortis as voiced and lenis/aspirated as voiceless; novice Japanese learners showed no significant production difference among the three categories (all long-lag VOT).
2002, 언어청각장애연구, 8 Japanese speakers: aspirated vs tense discriminated well, plain hard to distinguish from the others; plain often heard as aspirated.

Lee, Yamaguchi & Fougeron (Interspeech 2022), French learners (not one of our L1s): lenis hardest; learners over-weight VOT vs f0; mastery needs re-weighting cues. Used only as general support for the f0 point.

Kim Jeong-hyo (2008, 한중인문학연구 24): Mongolian learners' phoneme-perception errors attributed to L1 interference; phonemes studied include ㅣ/ㅡ, ㅗ/ㅜ, tense consonants, ㅈ/ㅊ, coda ㅇ/ㄴ. Abstract gives no error rates.

en.tendency: Learners vary widely: some use both VOT and F0 for the 3-way contrast, some rely on one cue, with less robust F0 use than natives.

zh.tendency: Tend to gain VOT control earlier than onset F0 control; the imbalance can hurt intelligibility.

ja.tendency: Novice learners tend to hear fortis as voiced and lenis/aspirated as voiceless; plain stops are the most often confused category in perception.

mn.tendency: Fortis consonants (경음) are among the phonemes reported as error-prone for Mongolian learners (abstract gives no direction of error).

topics.disagreement: Which pair is hardest for English L1 is reported as debated (fortis-lenis vs lenis-aspirated) in secondary text seen in search results only; not verified in an opened page.

topics.title_en: Final consonants (받침) sound like only 7 sounds
topics.tip_en: At the end of a syllable (or before a consonant), Korean has only 7 sounds: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ. Spellings like ㅅ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ all sound like ㄷ, and the final stop is not released (no puff of air).
topics.drill_en: Say 낫, 낮, 낯, 낱 aloud: they should all sound the same, [낟], with your tongue stopping at the ridge and no burst.

sources.what_it_says: National Institute of Korean Language (최혜원, 표준 발음): in syllable-final position consonants are realized only as ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ; ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ become [ㄷ], ㄱ ㄲ become [ㄱ], ㅍ becomes [ㅂ]. (Fetched via summarizer; 'unreleased' not confirmed there.)

Kim Jooyeon (2016, Phonetics & Speech Sciences 8(4)): Mandarin allows only /n,ŋ/ codas; 21 beginner Chinese learners improved coda perception over a year, with significant change for /n,p,k,m/ but not /l,ŋ,t/.
Kim Jeong-hyo (2008): coda ㅇ (and ㄴ) listed among phonemes where Mongolian learners show perception errors; no detail in abstract.

zh.tendency: Mandarin has few codas (only nasals), so identifying Korean codas, esp. stop codas, is a reported difficulty that improves with study; /l, ŋ, t/ did not change significantly in one year.

mn.tendency: Coda ㅇ/ㄴ is reported as an error-prone area (abstract-level only).

topics.disagreement: No disagreement found. Unreleased quality of 7 codas comes from general phonetics, not verified in an opened page.

topics.tip_en: ㅓ and ㅗ are different vowels. For ㅗ, round and push your lips forward; for ㅓ, keep your lips relaxed and mouth more open. Compare 어 and 오 in pairs.
topics.drill_en: Alternate 어-오-어-오 slowly in a mirror: lips should round only for 오.

sources.what_it_says: Ganieva (2018/19 master's thesis, Gangneung-Wonju Univ.): reports Russian-speaking learners have trouble distinguishing ㅓ from ㅗ (and ㅔ from ㅐ). Article-level data not seen.

ru.tendency: Reported difficulty telling ㅓ from ㅗ apart (thesis abstract).

topics.disagreement: Articulatory description in the tip (lip rounding) is not from an opened source; teaching materials seen only as search snippets (wikidocs, happycampus) said English/Japanese/Chinese learners confuse ㅓ/ㅗ but pages could not be opened.

topics.tip_en: ㅡ is said with lips spread flat; ㅜ needs rounded, pushed-out lips. If your lips are round, you are making ㅜ.
topics.drill_en: Say 으-우-으-우 while watching your lips: flat for 으, round for 우.

sources.what_it_says: Kim Jeong-hyo (2008): vowel pairs ㅣ/ㅡ and ㅗ/ㅜ studied for Mongolian learners' perception errors (not ㅡ/ㅜ directly).

topics.disagreement: NOT SOURCED: no opened page addresses ㅡ/ㅜ. Lip-shape tip is general phonetics. Japanese ㅜ/ㅡ difficulty claim only appears in unopenable wikidocs.net/181132 (teaching material, not research).

topics.tip_en: Korean ㄹ is one sound with two forms: a quick tap between vowels (like the 'tt' in 'butter') and a lateral [l] at the end of a syllable. It is not English r vs l.
topics.drill_en: Say 라디오, 이름, 달, 말: tap on 라/리, tongue stays on the ridge for 달/말.

sources.what_it_says: Chung (2005, English Language & Literature Teaching 11(2)): in standard Seoul Korean a liquid is realized as [l] or [ɾ] in complementary distribution; flap between vowels, lateral in geminates; Japanese has a single liquid, usually a flap. (Read via downloaded PDF; paper is about Korean/Japanese learners of English.)
Yang, Ryu & Chung (APSIPA 2015): corpus of Chinese learners' Korean; liquid substitutions reported as the most salient segmental variation. Exact percentages garbled in abstract, not quoted.
Sookmyung study (2016): multinational learners; ㄹ accuracy higher in form-focused tasks; intermediate learners least accurate; errors in free speech at all levels.

zh.tendency: Liquid substitution (flap vs lateral confusions) is the most salient segmental variation in a corpus of Chinese learners' Korean.

topics.disagreement: Cornell Whitman review snippet and others unopened. Tip's 'tt in butter' analogy is from an EPG abstract seen in search results only; treat as unverified.

topics.title_en: Linking final consonant to a following vowel (연음)
topics.tip_en: When a syllable ending in a consonant is followed by a vowel, the consonant moves over to start the next syllable: 음악 sounds like [으막], 꽃이 like [꼬치]. Do not pause between the syllables.
topics.drill_en: Read 밥을, 옷이, 책은 and check each final consonant is said at the start of the next syllable: [바블] [오시] [채근].

sources.what_it_says: National Institute of Korean Language: a hidden final consonant 'comes alive as the first sound of the next syllable' when followed by a vowel-initial particle; example 빗이 pronounced [비시].
Lee Hye-jeong (2015, 이화어문논집 35): Vietnamese learners had high error rates on all phonological phenomena tested; for 연음, double codas had more errors than single codas.

vi.tendency: High error rates on 연음 reported, higher for double (겹받침) than single codas.

topics.disagreement: Examples 음악[으막], 책은[채근] are from standard rule 13 knowledge, not seen in the opened page (only 빗이[비시] confirmed).

topics.title_en: Nasalisation: ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ before ㄴ ㅁ (국물 -> 궁물)
topics.tip_en: A final ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ turns into a nasal when a ㄴ or ㅁ follows: 국물 is [궁물], 앞마당 is [암마당]. Say it as a nasal in the same place of the mouth.
topics.drill_en: Say 국물, 옷맵시, 앞마당 and check you hum (nasal) at the syllable break: [궁물] [온맵씨] [암마당].

sources.what_it_says: National Institute of Korean Language (최혜원, 2004): final ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ are pronounced [ㅇ ㄴ ㅁ] before ㄴ ㅁ; examples 국물[궁물], 옷맵시[온맵씨], 꽃망울[꼰망울], 앞마당[암마당]; also applies across word boundaries.
Han (2011, Phonetics & Speech Sciences 3(1)): 12 Chinese learners nasalized word-final obstruents in only ~11.7% of obstruent+nasal sequences (beginners ~7%, intermediate ~16%) vs 100% for natives.
Lee Hye-jeong (2015): among phonological phenomena tested, nasalisation had the highest error rate for Vietnamese learners.

zh.tendency: Tend to under-apply nasalisation across word boundaries (about 12% in one study) compared with native speakers.

vi.tendency: Nasalisation had the highest error rate among phenomena tested.

topics.title_en: Vowel length is not needed (modern Seoul Korean)
topics.tip_en: You do not need to hold vowels long or short to be understood. Most Seoul speakers no longer use vowel length to tell words apart, so focus on the vowel quality and the consonants instead.
topics.drill_en: Say 눈 (eye) and 눈 (snow) the same way; context, not length, tells them apart.

sources.what_it_says: Kim & Park (2019, 언어와 문화 15(3)): length reportedly in decline since the 1960s; among Seoul/Gyeonggi speakers only some distinguished it; perception-realisation match ~1% vs 75% in a late-1980s experiment; 'vowel length in Korean appears to be in the last stage of loss'.

Kim & Oh (2015, English21 28(4)): ㅔ and ㅐ were once distinct but modern speakers no longer distinguish them; English learners did not separate them in duration or spectra, advanced Chinese learners over-distinguished (hypercorrection).

en.tendency: For the merged vowels ㅔ/ㅐ, English learners did not differentiate them, which matches current Korean usage.

zh.tendency: Advanced Chinese learners tended to over-distinguish ㅔ from ㅐ.

topics.disagreement: Phonemic status of length is disputed among linguists (seen in search snippet only). Official 표준 발음법 still lists long vowels (not verified in an opened page). Tendency by L1 for length itself: none found.

unverified: Official 표준 발음법 articles 6-13, 18 verbatim: korean.go.kr rule pages returned wrong content; only 2 NIKL commentary articles (1999, 2004) opened.
'Unreleased' articulation of final stops: not stated in any opened page.
English L1 on codas, nasalisation, liaison, liquids, ㅓ/ㅗ, ㅡ/ㅜ: no opened source. Park 2012 JASA (English learners' vowels) only seen via search summary.
Chang 2010 (English) and Holliday 2015 (Mandarin) stop papers only via search summaries; sagepub/soas pages 403.
Japanese on vowels (ㅓ/ㅗ, ㅡ/ㅜ): wikidocs.net/181132 teaching material and Ewha thesis 241046 returned 403/503.
Vietnamese coda/stops/vowels: Ajou repository (aurora.ajou.ac.kr/handle/2018.oak/24486) did not load; claims there are unverified.
Russian: SNU thesis (s-space 10371/144440) and Ewha 245975 did not load; KCI diphthong paper (ART002499241) opened but is about /w/ diphthongs only, not among the 8 topics.
Mongolian: only one 2008 abstract (Kim Jeong-hyo) with no data.
